name: Karl Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a typical factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a plastic pipe extrusion line. The hot plastic comes through a die, cools in a water bath, and a saw cuts each pipe to length. I watch wall thickness and puller speed, and I have a vocational certificate plus ten years of mistakes to tell me when a measurement is drifting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What fills the rest of your week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Anna keeps books for local businesses, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. The factory pays a fairly ordinary operator wage, and we have about three months of expenses saved. On weekends I repair old workshop tools and sell them online, which brings a small extra amount. I use AI every day to search manuals and write listings, but I still test a drill before selling it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my line crew that AI is a handy search tool and no miracle. A pipe with a thin wall still fails a gauge test even if the listing sounds brilliant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extrusion wage looks safe if AI mostly levels off. Our three-month reserve covers a short surprise, and a few other plants are nearby. I would be a little bored that the tools did not improve more, but the mortgage matters more than my curiosity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the pipe line running and continue fixing old drills on Saturdays. From each newly paid tool sale I would transfer a fixed share of net profit to the household reserve after parts and postage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income in this picture. My hands still know more than the AI search box about a worn bearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What tool sale stands out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An old pillar drill came from a farm shed with a dead switch. I fitted a safe replacement, tested it with my daughter beside me and sold it to a mechanic. The profit paid for her school trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move tool profit to savings now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The repair work is small but real, and our mortgage has no interest in whether a drill sells late. A fixed transfer from a paid sale is easier for me to keep than a vague plan. Anna can see it in the books.

say: I would **tell** the crew AI search helps, but measured pipe walls still decide whether we ship.
I would **describe** the tools as useful without promising a factory revolution.
think: The **pipe** wage looks secure, and nearby plants give some backup.
I **like** AI experiments but would take a steady mortgage over a cleverer search box.
do: **Keep** operating the pipe extrusion line and testing wall thickness.
**Repair** and sell old workshop tools on Saturdays.
**Transfer** part of each paid tool-sale profit to new household savings.
feel: **Calm** about income, a little bored by the plateau.
S0.quote: A pipe with a thin wall still fails a gauge test even if the listing sounds brilliant.
fieldNote: **Karl** uses AI daily for manuals and sales listings but relies on physical gauge and tool tests.
He **has** a three-month cushion, typical factory pay and some nearby options, so a plateau feels secure.
**New** household saving comes from net profit on additional paid tool sales.

steps.text: Keep operating the pipe line and testing wall thickness
Repair and sell old workshop tools on Saturdays
Transfer part of each paid tool-sale profit into household savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the supervisor to show us which ordering and shift-planning tasks are moving onto software. If a new robot palletiser is proposed later, operators should see the safety plan and have first shot at training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use the present palletiser and know its faults, so I might be useful on a new cell. But if software shortens the shift roster, even I could lose hours. Anna’s book work may also be changed by AI, which makes a pleasant technical upgrade a household question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a paid supplier course on the new palletiser if the factory offers a supervised place with my present hours and wage, and take it if those terms are written. I would practise a new AI line-scheduling tool on a test plan only if the company provides access and a supervisor checks it. I would keep selling repaired tools while the staffing plan is unsettled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our combined hours, though I would enjoy learning the cell. I need the palletiser job’s pay terms before calling it progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the supplier course need to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe isolation before touching a stopped arm, then fault finding under supervision. I will not learn that by watching a video after a twelve-hour shift. The course needs paid time and a real place on the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the new cell place is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current extrusion job and check posted operator vacancies at nearby plants. I would apply only if the pay covers our mortgage and the shift fits the children’s pickup. That search is separate from a course I cannot take.

say: I would **ask** for the software roster plan and a safe training offer before a new palletiser.
**Operators** should have first chance at a paid supervised cell place.
think: My **palletiser** experience helps, but shorter factory hours remain possible.
**Anna’s** bookkeeping hours could also change as AI takes planning and checking work.
do: **Take** paid supervised supplier training if offered with current hours and wage.
**Practise** a new AI line-scheduling tool on test plans if approved and checked.
**Keep** Saturday tool sales while the plant decides staffing.
feel: **Anxious** about two possible wage cuts, but keen to learn the cell.
S1.quote: I need the palletiser job’s pay terms before calling it progress.
fieldNote: **Karl** is eager to learn early but requires paid supervised instruction and written hours and wage terms.
His **wife’s** checking work is exposed to AI sooner than physical pipe handling, making the household risk broader.
If **no** training place appears, his local operator search has independent posted pay and school-hour conditions.

steps.text: Take paid supervised palletiser course if offered with current hours and wage
Practise new AI line-scheduling tool on test plans only if approved and checked
Keep selling repaired workshop tools while staffing is unsettled
Check posted nearby operator jobs if no cell place appears and pay and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my family that AGI could do Anna’s checking and our factory scheduling by 2028, while capable robots able to run the pipe line arrive around 2031. I would ask the plant for a dated installation plan, not a sales slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a major reduction in my extrusion shifts once robots can clear jams and test pipes around 2031. Anna’s book clients might cut her hours even earlier, and old tools could be repaired by machines too. Three months saved is not much against two lost wages, and I would lie awake calculating the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop buying extra tool stock this month and sell the repaired stock already in my shed, using new sale profit to add to savings. Anna and I would cut the planned holiday and ask the plant about paid redeployment training. If my hours are cut, I would apply for posted local maintenance work only if paid safety training is offered and wages cover our mortgage and school travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about both incomes. I can move quickly, but the bills will keep coming. A box of old tools will not pay every mortgage instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy cheap robot arms if other factories close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after someone pays me for a repair job and I have checked the arm’s safety records. I would not gamble the mortgage reserve on a bargain machine. There may be a market, but the first customer has to be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the holiday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we are doing day trips this year because both work schedules may change. I would not tell them a robot is certain to take our home. Anna and I would do the figures before bringing them into the worry.

say: I would **ask** for factory robot dates and distinguish 2028 software from around-2031 hands-on change.
**Both** pipe work and family bookkeeping could lose paid hours.
think: I **expect** major extrusion shift cuts around 2031 and possible earlier bookkeeping loss.
**Three** months saved is too little if both wages weaken.
do: **Stop** buying old tool stock and sell repaired stock already held.
**Cancel** the planned holiday and add new tool-sale profit to savings.
**Apply** for posted maintenance work only with paid safety instruction and mortgage-covering wages.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected household wage loss and awake calculating mortgage payments.
S2.quote: A box of old tools will not pay every mortgage instalment.
fieldNote: **Karl** expects his wife’s bookkeeping exposure with 2028 AGI before robots threaten his pipe line around 2031.
He **stops** tying up cash in tool stock but saves only from actual new sale profit.
The **maintenance** search needs a real posted vacancy, paid safety instruction and enough wages for mortgage and school travel.

steps.text: Stop buying extra workshop tools for resale this month
Transfer net profit from new paid tool sales into savings
Apply for posted local maintenance work if hours cut with paid safety training and bill-covering wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift that five years is enough to learn cell repair before the plant replaces the hands-on work. AGI in 2031 can handle scheduling; capable robots on the floor follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 51 when those robots arrive I might lose the operator roster, even if I know the old palletiser well. A small robot-repair service could help, but I would not put my mortgage behind a customer who has not called. Anna’s books and the children’s school hours still shape the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take an accredited evening robot-maintenance course next year if the fee fits after bills and school pickup is covered, and ask for a paid supervised cell shift at the plant if one is offered. After training, I would take weekend repair bookings only when a customer pays a deposit and the job meets safety rules. I would apply for a posted plant maintenance vacancy if the pay covers our mortgage; until offered, I would keep my extrusion shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing the roster, but five years gives me time to prove whether repair customers exist. I can keep the family reserve intact while testing one job at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a safe repair job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cell with its power isolated, a documented fault and an owner who lets me work under the proper safety procedure. I would not let a child help with a robot arm just because she helped paint a drill. Some tools belong in the shed, others do not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the evening course is too expensive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the factory shifts and look at posted operator roles nearby if the roster starts shrinking. I would apply only where the wage covers our mortgage and the school-hour travel works. I would not borrow for a course without paid customers or a real job route.

say: I would **ask** for accredited maintenance study and paid supervised plant practice.
A **five-year** runway lets workers test repair demand before capable robots arrive.
think: The 2034 **hands-on** robots may remove my operator roster at age 51.
A **repair** service needs paying customers and safe jobs before it can support the mortgage.
do: **Take** affordable accredited robot-maintenance training with pickup covered and paid supervised cell practice if offered.
**Take** deposited weekend robot repairs under documented safety rules after training.
**Apply** for posted mortgage-covering maintenance work; if course unaffordable, seek posted operator work with school-compatible travel.
feel: **Anxious** about the roster, with time to test customers without risking the reserve.
S3.quote: I would not put my mortgage behind a customer who has not called.
fieldNote: **Karl’s** adaptive plan depends on new controls knowledge, paid supervised practice and a customer deposit.
He **distinguishes** a safe robot repair from his informal old-tool work at home.
His **fallback** operator search is separate from an unaffordable course and still tests posted pay and school travel.

steps.text: Take affordable maintenance course with pickup and paid supervised cell practice if offered
Take deposited weekend robot repairs only with documented safety rules after training
Apply for posted plant maintenance job after training only if pay covers mortgage
Apply for posted operator work if course unaffordable and pay and school travel fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the factory that ten years is long enough to offer real apprenticeships and publish the robot roster before it changes jobs. I would also tell my neighbours that a repair business needs invoices, not only enthusiasm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036 and 56 when capable robots follow around 2039. The pipe line could last until then, but Anna’s bookkeeping could change earlier and our mortgage will still need paid work. I want a second trade ready before the factory makes the choice for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take an accredited maintenance course within the next two years if it fits our budget and school pickup, and keep the extrusion wage while doing deposited weekend robot repairs under proper safety rules. I would add a fixed part of each new repair payment to savings after materials. In the first year after 2036, I would apply for a posted local maintenance role only if the wage and hours cover our mortgage; I would not leave the pipe line before an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the eventual roster cut, although I have time to build real repair work. A written contract would settle my nerves more than a workshop full of spare arms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you open a repair workshop before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after repeat customers pay enough to cover rent, insurance and the mortgage without dipping into the three-month reserve. A Saturday bench is cheaper than a shop lease. Anna would want two years of figures, and I agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask for in an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time on a real cell, a safe isolation lesson and a posted job at the end. I would tell the supervisor that a photograph beside a robot is not training. Our children should see skilled work paid for properly.

say: I would **ask** the factory for paid apprenticeships and a dated robot staffing plan.
A **robot-repair** shop needs paid customers before anyone signs a lease.
think: At 53 in 2036, **AGI** may reach Anna’s bookkeeping before my physical pipe work.
At 56 **near** 2039, capable robots could shrink my line roster despite another trade.
do: **Take** affordable accredited maintenance training while keeping factory wages.
Do **deposited** weekend robot repairs under safety rules and save from new payments.
**Apply** for posted local maintenance work only with mortgage-covering wages and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about later income risk, but able to build evidence before leaving.
S4.quote: I would tell the supervisor that a photograph beside a robot is not training.
fieldNote: **Karl** likes new tools but requires paying repeat customers before replacing a steady wage with workshop rent.
His **training** must fit household fees and pickup; repair bookings require deposits and safety rules.
He would **add** to savings from new repair payments, then test posted maintenance wages and hours before leaving the line.

steps.text: Take accredited maintenance course if fees and school pickup fit
Take deposited weekend robot repair work under documented safety rules
Transfer fixed part of each new repair payment into savings after materials

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year AGI picture worries me most. Anna’s bookkeeping might lose work in 2028, while capable robots could cut my pipe shifts around 2031. Paid safety training and a real local maintenance vacancy would help us keep the mortgage covered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the old machines when a factory installs new ones. I repair old drills now, and I might find paid robot work later, but I would want a customer deposit before buying a single arm.

headlineQuote: I would want a customer deposit before buying a single arm.
portrait: **Karl** Zhang, 43, runs a plastic pipe extrusion line, holds a vocational certificate and uses AI daily for manuals and tool listings.
He and his **bookkeeper** wife Anna share two school-age children, a mortgage and about three months of expenses saved.
He **repairs** and sells old workshop tools, enjoys new machines, but tests sales and repair work against real customers.
**Thinking** AGI could threaten Anna’s books before capable robots reach Karl’s pipe line around 2031, which alarms him.
He **seeks** accredited maintenance training, safe deposited robot repairs and posted mortgage-covering work before leaving factory wages.
biggestWorry: The 2028 **AGI** scenario could cut Anna’s bookkeeping before around-2031 robots reduce his pipe shifts.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** safety training and a posted local maintenance job with mortgage-covering wages would help.
